author: Brady Middlebrook
title: Prop. C necessary but not enough, housing advocates say - NewsBreak
text:
By Brady Middlebrook ,
18 hours ago
District 7 Supervisor Myrna Melgar is seen in May introducing Proposition C, her charter-amendment measure that would increase annual contributions to the Housing Trust Fund. By By Patrick Hoge | Examiner staff writer
As Election Day approaches and well-funded committees argue over contentious proposals on San Francisco’s ballot, one measure has enjoyed rare near-unanimous support from progressives and moderates alike.
Proposition C, introduced by District 7 Supervisor Myrna Melgar in May , has the backing of nearly all The City’s affordable-housing organizations. It is also backed by the entire Board of Supervisors, which unanimously approved it for the ballot in July.
The proposal would amend the City Charter to gradually increase annual contributions from the general fund to the Housing Trust Fund from $52 million to $125 million over a period of several years.
The Housing Trust Fund is used to support the creation, acquisition and rehabilitation of affordable housing, as well as assist with down payments for affordable-home ownership.
If the measure passes, The City would increase its annual contributions to the trust fund by allocating a portion of future property-tax growth until contributions reach $125 million.
After that point, the trust fund would increase at the same rate as general-fund discretionary revenue up to 3% per year, through 2058.
Mayor Daniel Lurie touted the proposed fund expansion as “transformative” in a May press release announcing the ballot measure. But affordable-housing groups acknowledge that the near-term effects on housing construction — as well as broader rent and affordability issues — would likely be minor.
They also agree that the fund expansion alone would not bring The City within reach of its state-mandated construction goal of 46,000 affordable units by 2031.
Still, backers say the funding measure is a step in the right direction and a reliable, risk-free way to make developers more competitive for other funding streams.
The ballot argument in favor of the measure claims it will “build and rehabilitate affordable housing, fund down payment assistance for teachers and first responders, provide rent assistance to prevent seniors from being displaced, convert vacant lots into real housing, and fund needed infrastructure.”
The argument in opposition — signed only by the San Francisco Republican Party — claims the Housing Trust Fund has been ineffective. It says the party opposes the measure because it will take money from the general fund and lacks concrete housing-construction targets.
“Prop C locks a growing share of the General Fund into a charter set-aside until 2058 at a time when The City is facing a structural deficit,” wrote Nick Berg, chairman of the SF Republican Party.
Rebecca Foster, CEO of the Housing Accelerator Fund — which has donated $400,000 to the yes on C campaign — said that given San Francisco’s recent budget issues, the fund’s gradual growth and the Board of Supervisors’ ability to freeze it in bad budget years makes Prop. C a fiscally responsible part of the solution to The City’s housing problems.
The organization has estimated the trust-fund expansion would support the production or preservation of at least 18,000 units over 30 years and provide eviction protection to thousands of renters.
Laura Foote, the executive director of YIMBY Action — the national parent organization of SF YIMBY — said she supports expanding the fund as a way to attract state and federal funding for developers, but she doesn’t see it as quite as consequential as Lurie implied.
“The City contributes a little bit of money,” to housing developments, Foote said, “and that often helps, and likes to determine who gets to apply for state funding as well as federal funding.”
But she said the potential effectiveness of Prop. C pales in comparison to Proposition 1 , a state measure that would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds for housing-affordability programs. She said it would have a much larger effect on affordable housing in The City than any local measure currently on the ballot.
Matt Regan, the chief policy officer at the Bay Area Council — a nonpartisan business association and public-policy organization — agreed that the reliably increasing contributions to the fund would help housing developers in San Francisco secure more outside funding and make developments more financially viable.
“That predictability really matters, because affordable housing projects rely on multiple funding sources, sometimes as many as a dozen,” Regan wrote in an email. “A dependable local commitment helps San Francisco projects be more competitive for state and federal funding.”
Brandon Powell, the Bay Area organizing director for YIMBY Action, said the organization supports the measure because it puts money into housing construction without increasing or levying new taxes.
While affordable-housing organizations agree that Prop. C is an important investment in affordable housing, they also say The City needs to be doing more to make development faster and easier. Supporters of the measure say San Francisco should streamline permitting and approval processes and lower taxes on housing developments.
Melgar announced in September that she is planning to propose legislation to establish a new Department of Housing Production and Preservation in an effort to coordinate and streamline housing development processes.
The department would expand the Mayor’s Office of Housing and Community Development into a standalone body to guide housing policy and consolidate housing functions that are currently scattered across multiple departments.
In the May press release, Melgar and Lurie also announced plans to issue $70 million in revenue bonds for housing preservation next year, which would be used to invest in protecting deed-restricted affordable housing and to acquire and convert private rentals into permanently affordable units.
“Right now in San Francisco, housing is not getting built at the pace we need, and the consequences are all around us,” Lurie said in the release. “We must take bold action.”
